items.stem: Which of the following best describes "quorum sensing"?
options: A process in bacteria in which signalling molecules accumulate as population density increases, triggering coordinated gene expression
A change in membrane potential from negative towards positive, caused by Na⁺ ions diffusing into the axon
A signalling chemical that binds specifically to a receptor
A transmembrane receptor that, when bound by a ligand such as insulin, phosphorylates tyrosine residues, starting a signalling cascade
items.answer: A process in bacteria in which signalling molecules accumulate as population density increases, triggering coordinated gene expression
items.markingKey: A. "quorum sensing" is a process in bacteria in which signalling molecules accumulate as population density increases, triggering coordinated gene expression.

items.stem: Distinguish between intracellular receptors and transmembrane receptors.
items.answer: Transmembrane receptors span the membrane and bind hydrophilic signals outside; intracellular receptors are inside the cell and bind hydrophobic signals such as steroids.
items.markingKey: Transmembrane receptors span the membrane and bind hydrophilic signals outside; intracellular receptors are inside the cell and bind hydrophobic signals such as steroids. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why can a single hormone have different effects on different tissues?
options: Hormones never act on more than one tissue.
Different tissues have different receptors and signalling pathways.
items.answer: Different tissues have different receptors and signalling pathways.
items.markingKey: D. Receptor-dependent.

items.stem: Calcium ions act as signals in muscle and neurones. What category of signal are they?
items.answer: second messengers / local signalling chemicals
items.markingKey: C. Intracellular signal.

items.stem:
Honeybees were fed sugar solution containing different concentrations of a neonicotinoid pesticide (ng per bee). The percentage of foraging bees that returned to the hive was recorded.

Dose / ng per bee | Bees returning / %
0 | 94
1 | 88
2 | 83
5 | 69
10 | 51
20 | 30

(a) State the percentage of bees returning at a dose of 10 ng per bee. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage change in return rate between 0 and 5 ng per bee. [2]
(c) Describe the relationship between dose and return rate. [2]
items.answer: (a) 51 % (b) -26.6 % (c) Return rate decreases as dose increases; the decrease is steepest at low doses / non-linear.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 51 (A1). (b) [2] (69 − 94)/94 × 100 (M1) = -26.6 % (A1). (c) [2] Negative relationship (A1); detail of trend (A1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Chemical signalling is a more effective method of communication than neural signalling."
items.answer: Each is effective for different purposes: chemical signals for widespread, sustained responses and nerves for rapid, precise ones.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: hormones reach all cells with receptors and give long-lasting coordinated responses (e.g. growth); chemical signalling is universal, even in bacteria. Arguments against: neural signalling is much faster and more precisely targeted; many responses need both, e.g. adrenaline release by nerves. Supported judgement: Each is effective for different purposes: chemical signals for widespread, sustained responses and nerves for rapid, precise ones.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A small protein signalling molecule, especially in the immune system, that acts locally on nearby cells"?
items.answer: cytokine
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of cytokine.

items.stem: Explain how quorum sensing allows bacteria to coordinate behaviour.
items.answer: Each bacterium secretes a signalling molecule (autoinducer); as population density increases its concentration rises; above a threshold it binds receptors and alters gene expression in all cells, e.g. switching on luciferase genes in Vibrio fischeri.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each bacterium secretes a signalling molecule (autoinducer); as population density increases its concentration rises; above a threshold it binds receptors and alters gene expression in all cells, e.g. switching on luciferase genes in Vibrio fischeri. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: How do neurotransmitters differ from hormones in the distance they act over?
options: Both act over the same distance.
Neurotransmitters act across a synapse (nanometres); hormones travel in blood throughout the body.
items.answer: Neurotransmitters act across a synapse (nanometres); hormones travel in blood throughout the body.
items.markingKey: C. Local vs long distance.

items.stem:
Glucose uptake (nmol per mg protein per min) was measured in fat cells (adipocytes) taken from people with normal insulin sensitivity and from people with insulin resistance, at different insulin concentrations.

Insulin / nmol dm⁻³ | Uptake – normal | Uptake – insulin resistant
0 | 1.5 | 1.5
0.1 | 2.9 | 1.6
1 | 8.0 | 2.3
10 | 11.4 | 5.4
100 | 12.0 | 7.8

(a) State the glucose uptake by normal cells at 1 nmol dm⁻³ insulin. [1]
(b) Calculate how many times greater the uptake by normal cells is at 100 nmol dm⁻³ insulin than with no insulin. [1]
(c) Calculate the percentage difference in uptake of insulin-resistant cells compared with normal cells at 1 nmol dm⁻³ insulin. [2]
items.answer: (a) 8.0 nmol mg⁻¹ min⁻¹ (b) 8.0 times (c) -71.2 %

items.stem:
The conduction speed of nerve impulses was measured in myelinated and unmyelinated axons of different diameters in a mammal.

Axon diameter / µm | Myelinated speed / m s⁻¹ | Unmyelinated speed / m s⁻¹
2 | 12 | 0.6
5 | 29 | 1.0
10 | 59 | 1.4
15 | 88 | 1.8
20 | 118 | 2.0

(a) State the conduction speed of a 10 µm myelinated axon. [1]
(b) Calculate how many times faster a 10 µm myelinated axon conducts than an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter. [1]
(c) Calculate the time taken for an impulse to travel 1.0 m along each type of 10 µm axon. [2]
items.answer: (a) 59 m s⁻¹ (b) 42 times (c) myelinated 16.9 ms; unmyelinated 714 ms

items.stem: Describe the different types of signalling chemicals and explain how receptors allow cells to respond to them.
items.answer: Types: hormones (peptide/steroid/amine), neurotransmitters, cytokines, calcium ions; quorum sensing autoinducers in bacteria. Receptors: specific proteins, complementary binding, reversible; transmembrane (insulin, adrenaline, acetylcholine) vs intracellular (steroids); localised vs distant effects; specificity of target cells.
items.markingKey: Types: hormones (peptide/steroid/amine), neurotransmitters, cytokines, calcium ions; quorum sensing autoinducers in bacteria. Receptors: specific proteins, complementary binding, reversible; transmembrane (insulin, adrenaline, acetylcholine) vs intracellular (steroids); localised vs distant effects; specificity of target cells.

items.stem: Which hormone acts through a tyrosine kinase receptor?
items.answer: insulin
items.markingKey: D. Insulin receptors autophosphorylate.

items.stem: Explain how insulin signals through a tyrosine kinase receptor.
items.answer: Insulin binds to the extracellular part of the receptor; the receptor subunits phosphorylate tyrosine residues on each other (autophosphorylation); relay proteins bind and are activated, starting a cascade; vesicles with GLUT4 move to and fuse with the membrane, increasing glucose uptake.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Insulin binds to the extracellular part of the receptor; the receptor subunits phosphorylate tyrosine residues on each other (autophosphorylation); relay proteins bind and are activated, starting a cascade; vesicles with GLUT4 move to and fuse with the membrane, increasing glucose uptake. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Aiko writes: "A signal is weakened at each step of a cascade." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Signalling cascades amplify the signal: each activated molecule activates many of the next.
items.markingKey: Signalling cascades amplify the signal: each activated molecule activates many of the next. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In a liver cell, one adrenaline–receptor complex activates 5 G proteins; each activates one adenylyl cyclase molecule, which produces 50 cAMP molecules; each cAMP (via protein kinase A) leads to activation of enzymes that release 500 glucose molecules from glycogen. Calculate the number of glucose molecules released per receptor activated and explain the significance of this.
items.answer: 125 000 glucose molecules; amplification gives a large, rapid response to a small amount of hormone
items.markingKey: 5 × 50 × 500 (M1) = 125 000 (A1); amplification by cascade – small hormone concentration gives large response (R1).

items.stem: Using type 2 diabetes and insulin resistance as an example, explain tyrosine kinase signalling.
items.answer: Target cells respond poorly to insulin even though insulin is present. Defects in the receptor or downstream pathway reduce GLUT4 movement to the membrane, so glucose uptake is reduced.
items.markingKey: Context (Target cells respond poorly to insulin even though insulin is present.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Defects in the receptor or downstream pathway reduce GLUT4 movement to the membrane, so glucose uptake is reduced. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to tyrosine kinase signalling.

items.stem: Compare the signal transduction pathways of adrenaline and insulin.
items.answer: Both bind surface receptors; adrenaline: GPCR, G protein, GTP, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, PKA cascade, glycogen breakdown; insulin: tyrosine kinase, autophosphorylation, relay proteins, GLUT4 vesicles fuse, glucose uptake; amplification; termination.
items.markingKey: Both bind surface receptors; adrenaline: GPCR, G protein, GTP, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, PKA cascade, glycogen breakdown; insulin: tyrosine kinase, autophosphorylation, relay proteins, GLUT4 vesicles fuse, glucose uptake; amplification; termination.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "second messenger".
items.answer: A small molecule such as cyclic AMP that relays a signal from a receptor to targets inside the cell
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a small molecule such as cyclic AMP that relays a signal from a receptor to targets inside the cell. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between tyrosine kinase receptors and G-protein-coupled receptors.
items.answer: GPCRs activate a G protein, which activates enzymes producing second messengers such as cAMP (e.g. adrenaline); tyrosine kinase receptors phosphorylate tyrosines on themselves when the ligand binds, activating relay proteins (e.g. insulin).
items.markingKey: GPCRs activate a G protein, which activates enzymes producing second messengers such as cAMP (e.g. adrenaline); tyrosine kinase receptors phosphorylate tyrosines on themselves when the ligand binds, activating relay proteins (e.g. insulin). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why must signalling pathways be switched off?
options: So cells respond only while the signal is present, allowing control.
items.answer: So cells respond only while the signal is present, allowing control.
items.markingKey: D. Termination.

items.stem: A mutation causes a G protein to remain permanently bound to GTP. What is the likely effect?
options: The signalling pathway stays switched on even without the ligand.
The pathway can never be activated.
items.answer: The signalling pathway stays switched on even without the ligand.
items.markingKey: B. Cholera toxin has a similar effect.

items.stem: "Signal transduction pathways are good targets for new drugs." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: They are excellent targets and many drugs act on them, but specificity and resistance are major challenges.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many drugs target GPCRs and kinases, e.g. beta blockers and kinase inhibitors in cancer; cascades offer several points of control. Arguments against: pathways are shared by many cell types, so drugs may have side effects; cells can bypass blocked steps, leading to resistance. Supported judgement: They are excellent targets and many drugs act on them, but specificity and resistance are major challenges. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "repolarisation".
items.answer: The return of membrane potential to a negative value, caused by K⁺ ions diffusing out of the axon
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the return of membrane potential to a negative value, caused by K⁺ ions diffusing out of the axon. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why does the membrane potential briefly become more negative than −70 mV after an action potential?
options: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels are slow to close, so excess K⁺ leaves (hyperpolarisation).
items.answer: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels are slow to close, so excess K⁺ leaves (hyperpolarisation).
items.markingKey: B. Overshoot of repolarisation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain how a resting potential is established and maintained.
items.answer: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in; the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ (leak channels), so K⁺ diffuses out; negatively charged proteins remain inside; result is about −70 mV inside relative to outside. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in; the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ (leak channels), so K⁺ diffuses out; negatively charged proteins remain inside; result is about −70 mV inside relative to outside. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to multiple sclerosis, explain how it illustrates the role of myelination.
items.answer: The immune system damages myelin in the brain and spinal cord, causing problems with movement and vision. Without myelin, saltatory conduction fails, so impulses slow or are blocked.
items.markingKey: Context (The immune system damages myelin in the brain and spinal cord, causing problems with movement and vision.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Without myelin, saltatory conduction fails, so impulses slow or are blocked. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of myelination.

items.stem: In multiple sclerosis the myelin sheath is damaged. Which effect is expected?
options: Slower or failed conduction of impulses along affected axons.
No change because myelin is not needed.
items.answer: Slower or failed conduction of impulses along affected axons.
items.markingKey: A. Loss of saltatory conduction.

items.stem: An impulse travels along a myelinated axon at 50 m s⁻¹. How long does it take to travel 0.9 m?
Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The all-or-nothing nature of action potentials limits the information a nerve can carry."
items.answer: All-or-nothing signals are reliable over long distances and frequency coding carries information, so it is not a serious limitation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: each impulse is the same size, so amplitude cannot carry information. Arguments against: information is coded by frequency of impulses and by which neurones fire; all-or-nothing signals do not fade with distance. Supported judgement: All-or-nothing signals are reliable over long distances and frequency coding carries information, so it is not a serious limitation.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of a neurone is related to its function.
items.answer: Dendrites receive signals; cell body with nucleus and many ribosomes; long axon carries impulses over distance; myelin and nodes allow saltatory conduction; axon terminals with vesicles release neurotransmitter; membrane with pumps and voltage-gated channels.
items.markingKey: Dendrites receive signals; cell body with nucleus and many ribosomes; long axon carries impulses over distance; myelin and nodes allow saltatory conduction; axon terminals with vesicles release neurotransmitter; membrane with pumps and voltage-gated channels.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The membrane potential (about −50 to −55 mV) that must be reached for voltage-gated sodium channels to open and an action potential to start"?
items.answer: threshold potential
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of threshold potential.

items.stem: Explain how a resting potential is established and maintained.
items.answer: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in; the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ (leak channels), so K⁺ diffuses out; negatively charged proteins remain inside; result is about −70 mV inside relative to outside.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in; the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ (leak channels), so K⁺ diffuses out; negatively charged proteins remain inside; result is about −70 mV inside relative to outside. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Nerve impulses are electrons flowing along the axon like a current in a wire." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Impulses are waves of depolarisation caused by movement of Na⁺ and K⁺ ions across the membrane.
items.markingKey: Impulses are waves of depolarisation caused by movement of Na⁺ and K⁺ ions across the membrane. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An impulse travels 0.89 m along a motor neurone from the spinal cord to a muscle in the foot in 17.6 ms. Calculate the conduction speed in m s⁻¹.
items.markingKey: Speed = distance/time = 0.89 m ÷ 0.0176 s (M1) = 50.6 m s⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the giant axon of the squid shows the effect of axon diameter on conduction speed.
items.answer: Unmyelinated axons up to 1 mm in diameter conduct impulses at about 25 m s⁻¹ for the escape response. Large diameter reduces resistance to local currents, increasing speed without myelin.
items.markingKey: Context (Unmyelinated axons up to 1 mm in diameter conduct impulses at about 25 m s⁻¹ for the escape response.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Large diameter reduces resistance to local currents, increasing speed without myelin. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effect of axon diameter on conduction speed.

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "A stronger stimulus produces larger action potentials." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Action potentials are all-or-nothing and always the same size; a stronger stimulus increases their frequency.
items.markingKey: Action potentials are all-or-nothing and always the same size; a stronger stimulus increases their frequency. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
The conduction speed of nerve impulses was measured in myelinated and unmyelinated axons of different diameters in a mammal.

Axon diameter / µm | Myelinated speed / m s⁻¹ | Unmyelinated speed / m s⁻¹
2 | 11 | 0.9
5 | 27 | 1.5
10 | 54 | 2.1
15 | 81 | 2.6
20 | 108 | 3.0

(a) State the conduction speed of a 10 µm myelinated axon. [1]
(b) Calculate how many times faster a 10 µm myelinated axon conducts than an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter. [1]
(c) Calculate the time taken for an impulse to travel 1.0 m along each type of 10 µm axon. [2]
(d) Describe the effect of axon diameter on conduction speed in myelinated axons. [2]
items.answer: (a) 54 m s⁻¹ (b) 26 times (c) myelinated 18.5 ms; unmyelinated 476 ms (d) Speed increases in proportion to diameter (approximately linear relationship).
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 54 (A1). (b) [1] 54/2.1 = 26 (A1). (c) [2] t = d/v: 1.0/54 = 18.5 ms (A1); 1.0/2.1 = 476 ms (A1). (d) [2] Positive relationship (A1); approximately proportional (A1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "acetylcholinesterase"?
options: A signalling chemical that binds specifically to a receptor
A transmembrane receptor that, when bound by a ligand such as insulin, phosphorylates tyrosine residues, starting a signalling cascade
An enzyme in the synaptic cleft that hydrolyses acetylcholine into acetate and choline, ending its action
A signalling chemical released from a presynaptic neurone that diffuses across a synapse to bind to receptors on a postsynaptic cell
items.answer: An enzyme in the synaptic cleft that hydrolyses acetylcholine into acetate and choline, ending its action
items.markingKey: C. "acetylcholinesterase" is an enzyme in the synaptic cleft that hydrolyses acetylcholine into acetate and choline, ending its action.

items.stem: Why does summation allow integration of information?
options: Every input causes an action potential.
Inhibitory inputs add to excitatory ones.
Only one synapse is active at a time.
Whether the postsynaptic neurone fires depends on the combined excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
items.answer: Whether the postsynaptic neurone fires depends on the combined excitatory and inhibitory inputs.
items.markingKey: D. Neurones integrate signals.

items.stem: Mei writes: "Painkillers work by repairing damaged tissue." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many painkillers, like endorphins, block transmission of pain signals at synapses or reduce production of chemicals that stimulate nociceptors.
items.markingKey: Many painkillers, like endorphins, block transmission of pain signals at synapses or reduce production of chemicals that stimulate nociceptors. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An insecticide inhibits acetylcholinesterase. What happens at synapses in insect muscles?
options: Acetylcholine accumulates, causing continuous stimulation and paralysis.
items.answer: Acetylcholine accumulates, causing continuous stimulation and paralysis.
items.markingKey: A. Organophosphates act like this.

items.stem: Several presynaptic neurones fire at once and the postsynaptic neurone reaches threshold. This is:
items.answer: spatial summation
items.markingKey: D. Several inputs at once.

items.stem: Explain how drugs and pesticides can affect synaptic transmission, using named examples.
items.answer: Mimic neurotransmitter (neonicotinoids on ACh receptors, irreversible); block receptors (curare); inhibit enzyme (organophosphates on AChE); block reuptake (cocaine, SSRIs); stimulate release; endorphins/opioids block pain; consequences.
items.markingKey: Mimic neurotransmitter (neonicotinoids on ACh receptors, irreversible); block receptors (curare); inhibit enzyme (organophosphates on AChE); block reuptake (cocaine, SSRIs); stimulate release; endorphins/opioids block pain; consequences.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The combined effect of several excitatory postsynaptic potentials, either from one neurone firing repeatedly (temporal) or from several neurones (spatial), to reach threshold"?
items.answer: summation
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of summation.

items.stem: Distinguish between inhibitory synapses and excitatory synapses.
items.answer: At excitatory synapses the neurotransmitter depolarises the postsynaptic membrane, making an action potential more likely; at inhibitory synapses it hyperpolarises the membrane, making one less likely.
items.markingKey: At excitatory synapses the neurotransmitter depolarises the postsynaptic membrane, making an action potential more likely; at inhibitory synapses it hyperpolarises the membrane, making one less likely. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using cocaine use as an example, explain the effect of drugs on synapses.
items.answer: Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake transporters in the brain’s reward pathway. Dopamine stays in the cleft longer, overstimulating postsynaptic receptors and causing euphoria and addiction.
items.markingKey: Context (Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake transporters in the brain’s reward pathway.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Dopamine stays in the cleft longer, overstimulating postsynaptic receptors and causing euphoria and addiction. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effect of drugs on synapses.

items.stem: A postsynaptic neurone has a resting potential of -70 mV and a threshold of -52 mV. Each EPSP depolarises it by 2.5 mV. Calculate the minimum number of EPSPs that must summate to trigger an action potential.
items.markingKey: Depolarisation needed = -52 − (-70) = 18 mV (M1); 18/2.5 = 7.20, round up → 8 (A1).

items.stem: "Drugs that act on synapses are too dangerous to use in medicine." Discuss.
items.answer: Synaptic drugs are essential in medicine, but their risks require careful control rather than avoidance.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many cause addiction or tolerance (e.g. opioids); side effects as synapses are widespread. Arguments against: anaesthetics, antidepressants and painkillers relieve great suffering; careful dosing and regulation reduce risks. Supported judgement: Synaptic drugs are essential in medicine, but their risks require careful control rather than avoidance. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which ions diffuse into the axon during depolarisation?
items.answer: sodium ions
items.markingKey: A. Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open.

items.stem: Which signalling chemical is a steroid hormone?
items.answer: testosterone
items.markingKey: C. Steroids are lipids.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The series of events by which a signal received by a receptor is converted into a response inside the cell"?
items.answer: signal transduction
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of signal transduction.

items.stem: Explain the events of synaptic transmission at a cholinergic synapse.
items.answer: Action potential arrives at presynaptic terminal; voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ diffuses in; vesicles fuse with membrane (exocytosis) releasing acetylcholine; ACh diffuses across cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane; Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ enters, depolarisation; ACh hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase; choline reabsorbed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Action potential arrives at presynaptic terminal; voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ diffuses in; vesicles fuse with membrane (exocytosis) releasing acetylcholine; ACh diffuses across cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane; Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ enters, depolarisation; ACh hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase; choline reabsorbed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between myelinated axons and unmyelinated axons.
items.answer: Myelinated axons conduct by saltatory conduction at up to about 100 m s⁻¹, with action potentials only at nodes of Ranvier; unmyelinated axons depolarise every part of the membrane and conduct at about 1 m s⁻¹.
items.markingKey: Myelinated axons conduct by saltatory conduction at up to about 100 m s⁻¹, with action potentials only at nodes of Ranvier; unmyelinated axons depolarise every part of the membrane and conduct at about 1 m s⁻¹. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "All hormones must enter cells to have an effect." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Protein/peptide hormones such as insulin bind to receptors on the cell surface and act through signal transduction without entering.
items.markingKey: Protein/peptide hormones such as insulin bind to receptors on the cell surface and act through signal transduction without entering. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: How is a G-protein signal switched off?
options: The G protein hydrolyses GTP to GDP and becomes inactive.
items.answer: The G protein hydrolyses GTP to GDP and becomes inactive.
items.markingKey: D. Intrinsic GTPase activity.

items.stem: Why is synaptic transmission slower than conduction along an axon?
options: Neurotransmitter release, diffusion and receptor binding take time (synaptic delay).
items.answer: Neurotransmitter release, diffusion and receptor binding take time (synaptic delay).
items.markingKey: D. Chemical step.

items.stem: Why do myelinated axons conduct faster than unmyelinated axons of the same diameter?
options: Depolarisation occurs only at nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse jumps between nodes.
Myelin conducts electricity like a wire.
Myelinated axons have more sodium channels along their whole length.
Myelin carries ions along the axon.
items.answer: Depolarisation occurs only at nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse jumps between nodes.
items.markingKey: A. Saltatory conduction.

items.stem: A drug binds to adrenaline receptors without activating them. What effect would it have?
options: It would block the response to adrenaline (antagonist).
It would increase the response to adrenaline.
It would have no effect at all.
items.answer: It would block the response to adrenaline (antagonist).
items.markingKey: B. Beta blockers work like this.

items.stem: A drug blocks adenylyl cyclase in liver cells. What is the effect of adrenaline?
options: Little or no glycogen breakdown because cAMP is not produced.
items.answer: Little or no glycogen breakdown because cAMP is not produced.
items.markingKey: C. Pathway blocked.

items.stem: Outline one way in which cocaine use shows the effect of drugs on synapses.
items.answer: Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake transporters in the brain’s reward pathway. Dopamine stays in the cleft longer, overstimulating postsynaptic receptors and causing euphoria and addiction.
items.markingKey: Context (Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake transporters in the brain’s reward pathway.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Dopamine stays in the cleft longer, overstimulating postsynaptic receptors and causing euphoria and addiction. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effect of drugs on synapses.

items.stem: An impulse travels 0.77 m along a sensory neurone from a fingertip to the spinal cord in 13.5 ms. Calculate the conduction speed in m s⁻¹. State, with a reason, whether the axon is likely to be myelinated.
items.answer: 57.0 m s⁻¹; myelinated – speeds above about 10 m s⁻¹ in vertebrates indicate saltatory conduction
items.markingKey: Speed = distance/time = 0.77 m ÷ 0.0135 s (M1) = 57.0 m s⁻¹ (A1). Reasoned deduction (R1).

items.stem: Briefly describe beta blockers prescribed for high blood pressure and explain what it reveals about receptor–ligand specificity.
items.answer: The drugs bind to β-adrenergic receptors in the heart without activating them. By occupying the receptors they block adrenaline binding and reduce heart rate.
items.markingKey: Context (The drugs bind to β-adrenergic receptors in the heart without activating them.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: By occupying the receptors they block adrenaline binding and reduce heart rate. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to receptor–ligand specificity.

items.stem: In a liver cell, one adrenaline–receptor complex activates 10 G proteins; each activates one adenylyl cyclase molecule, which produces 10 cAMP molecules; each cAMP (via protein kinase A) leads to activation of enzymes that release 10 glucose molecules from glycogen. Calculate the number of glucose molecules released per receptor activated and explain the significance of this.
items.answer: 1 000 glucose molecules; amplification gives a large, rapid response to a small amount of hormone
items.markingKey: 10 × 10 × 10 (M1) = 1 000 (A1); amplification by cascade – small hormone concentration gives large response (R1).

items.stem: Curare blocks acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions. What is the effect?
options: Muscles are paralysed because ACh cannot depolarise the muscle membrane.
items.answer: Muscles are paralysed because ACh cannot depolarise the muscle membrane.
items.markingKey: C. Receptor antagonist.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The all-or-nothing nature of action potentials limits the information a nerve can carry."
items.answer: All-or-nothing signals are reliable over long distances and frequency coding carries information, so it is not a serious limitation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: each impulse is the same size, so amplitude cannot carry information. Arguments against: information is coded by frequency of impulses and by which neurones fire; all-or-nothing signals do not fade with distance. Supported judgement: All-or-nothing signals are reliable over long distances and frequency coding carries information, so it is not a serious limitation.

items.stem:
Honeybees were fed sugar solution containing different concentrations of a neonicotinoid pesticide (ng per bee). The percentage of foraging bees that returned to the hive was recorded.

Dose / ng per bee | Bees returning / %
0 | 86
1 | 79
2 | 75
5 | 64
10 | 51
20 | 28

(a) State the percentage of bees returning at a dose of 10 ng per bee. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage change in return rate between 0 and 5 ng per bee. [2]
(c) Describe the relationship between dose and return rate. [2]
(d) Explain how neonicotinoids affect synaptic transmission in insects. [3]
items.answer: (a) 51 % (b) -25.6 % (c) Return rate decreases as dose increases; the decrease is steepest at low doses / non-linear. (d) They bind to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on postsynaptic membranes; are not broken down by acetylcholinesterase; cause continuous depolarisation / overstimulation; disrupting nervous control.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 51 (A1). (b) [2] (64 − 86)/86 × 100 (M1) = -25.6 % (A1). (c) [2] Negative relationship (A1); detail of trend (A1). (d) [3] Binds ACh receptors (A1); not hydrolysed by AChE (A1); continuous stimulation (A1).

items.stem:
Glucose uptake (nmol per mg protein per min) was measured in fat cells (adipocytes) taken from people with normal insulin sensitivity and from people with insulin resistance, at different insulin concentrations.

Insulin / nmol dm⁻³ | Uptake – normal | Uptake – insulin resistant
0 | 1.4 | 1.4
0.1 | 2.4 | 1.5
1 | 6.9 | 2.1
10 | 11.3 | 4.9
100 | 12.2 | 7.6

(a) State the glucose uptake by normal cells at 1 nmol dm⁻³ insulin. [1]
(b) Calculate how many times greater the uptake by normal cells is at 100 nmol dm⁻³ insulin than with no insulin. [1]
(c) Calculate the percentage difference in uptake of insulin-resistant cells compared with normal cells at 1 nmol dm⁻³ insulin. [2]
(d) Compare the responses of the two types of cell to insulin. [3]
items.answer: (a) 6.9 nmol mg⁻¹ min⁻¹ (b) 8.7 times (c) -69.6 % (d) Both show increasing uptake with insulin that levels off; resistant cells have similar uptake without insulin but lower uptake at every insulin concentration and need higher insulin for a response.

items.stem: Explain how a nerve impulse is transmitted across a synapse and how the signal is terminated.
items.answer: AP at terminal; voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ influx; vesicles exocytosis; ACh diffuses; binds receptors; ligand-gated Na⁺ channels; depolarisation/EPSP; threshold, summation; acetylcholinesterase hydrolysis; choline reabsorbed and recycled; ATP needed; one-way.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "myelin sheath"?
options: A junction between two neurones, or between a neurone and an effector cell, across which signals are passed by neurotransmitters
A signalling chemical secreted by endocrine glands into the blood and transported to target cells elsewhere in the body
A transmembrane receptor that, when bound by a ligand such as insulin, phosphorylates tyrosine residues, starting a signalling cascade
Layers of plasma membrane of Schwann cells wrapped around an axon, which insulate it and allow saltatory conduction
items.answer: Layers of plasma membrane of Schwann cells wrapped around an axon, which insulate it and allow saltatory conduction
items.markingKey: D. "myelin sheath" is layers of plasma membrane of Schwann cells wrapped around an axon, which insulate it and allow saltatory conduction.

items.stem: Define the term "hormone".
items.answer: A signalling chemical secreted by endocrine glands into the blood and transported to target cells elsewhere in the body
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a signalling chemical secreted by endocrine glands into the blood and transported to target cells elsewhere in the body. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "G-protein-coupled receptor"?
options: A neurotransmitter that makes the postsynaptic membrane more negative (hyperpolarised), so an action potential is less likely
A small protein signalling molecule, especially in the immune system, that acts locally on nearby cells
A sensory receptor that detects stimuli that could damage tissue and gives the sensation of pain
A transmembrane receptor that, when a ligand binds, activates a G protein inside the cell, which then activates other proteins
items.answer: A transmembrane receptor that, when a ligand binds, activates a G protein inside the cell, which then activates other proteins
items.markingKey: D. "G-protein-coupled receptor" is a transmembrane receptor that, when a ligand binds, activates a G protein inside the cell, which then activates other proteins.

items.stem: Distinguish between spatial summation and temporal summation.
items.answer: Temporal summation is the adding of EPSPs from one presynaptic neurone firing repeatedly in quick succession; spatial summation is the adding of EPSPs from several presynaptic neurones firing at the same time.
items.markingKey: Temporal summation is the adding of EPSPs from one presynaptic neurone firing repeatedly in quick succession; spatial summation is the adding of EPSPs from several presynaptic neurones firing at the same time. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between repolarisation and depolarisation.
items.answer: Depolarisation is caused by Na⁺ moving in through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, making the inside positive; repolarisation is caused by K⁺ moving out through voltage-gated K⁺ channels, making the inside negative again.
items.markingKey: Depolarisation is caused by Na⁺ moving in through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, making the inside positive; repolarisation is caused by K⁺ moving out through voltage-gated K⁺ channels, making the inside negative again. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why can insulin not cross the plasma membrane but oestradiol can?
options: Insulin is a large polar protein; oestradiol is a small lipid-soluble steroid.
items.answer: Insulin is a large polar protein; oestradiol is a small lipid-soluble steroid.
items.markingKey: C. Lipid solubility determines membrane crossing.

items.stem: Tomás writes: "Adrenaline enters liver cells and breaks down glycogen directly." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Adrenaline binds to a surface receptor; the signal is relayed by a G protein and cAMP, which activate enzymes that break down glycogen.
items.markingKey: Adrenaline binds to a surface receptor; the signal is relayed by a G protein and cAMP, which activate enzymes that break down glycogen. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Action potentials jump across the synaptic cleft." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The signal crosses the cleft chemically, as neurotransmitter diffusing to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.
items.markingKey: The signal crosses the cleft chemically, as neurotransmitter diffusing to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why does an action potential travel in one direction only along an axon?
options: Ions only flow towards the cell body.
The region behind the impulse is in its refractory period, with Na⁺ channels inactivated.
items.answer: The region behind the impulse is in its refractory period, with Na⁺ channels inactivated.
items.markingKey: D. Refractory period.

items.stem: "A receptor permanently binds its ligand." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Ligand–receptor binding is reversible, allowing signals to be switched off.
items.markingKey: Ligand–receptor binding is reversible, allowing signals to be switched off. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which type 2 diabetes and insulin resistance shows tyrosine kinase signalling.
items.answer: Target cells respond poorly to insulin even though insulin is present. Defects in the receptor or downstream pathway reduce GLUT4 movement to the membrane, so glucose uptake is reduced.
items.markingKey: Context (Target cells respond poorly to insulin even though insulin is present.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Defects in the receptor or downstream pathway reduce GLUT4 movement to the membrane, so glucose uptake is reduced. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to tyrosine kinase signalling.

items.stem: A postsynaptic neurone has a resting potential of -68 mV and a threshold of -52 mV. Each EPSP depolarises it by 5 mV. Calculate the minimum number of EPSPs that must summate to trigger an action potential.
items.markingKey: Depolarisation needed = -52 − (-68) = 16 mV (M1); 16/5 = 3.20, round up → 4 (A1).

items.stem: An impulse travels 0.60 m from the spinal cord to a toe in 8.0 ms. What is the conduction speed?
items.answer: 75 m s⁻¹

items.stem: A hormone is injected and acts within seconds on liver cells without entering them. Which is most likely?
options: a peptide/amine hormone such as adrenaline binding a surface receptor
items.answer: a peptide/amine hormone such as adrenaline binding a surface receptor
items.markingKey: A. Rapid surface action.

items.stem: A student claims: "A signal is weakened at each step of a cascade." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Signalling cascades amplify the signal: each activated molecule activates many of the next.
items.markingKey: Signalling cascades amplify the signal: each activated molecule activates many of the next. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Each EPSP depolarises a postsynaptic neurone by 4 mV from a resting potential of −70 mV. Threshold is −55 mV. How many EPSPs must summate to start an action potential?
items.markingKey: D. 15 mV needed; 15/4 = 3.75, so 4 EPSPs.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Chemical signalling is a more effective method of communication than neural signalling."
items.answer: Each is effective for different purposes: chemical signals for widespread, sustained responses and nerves for rapid, precise ones.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: hormones reach all cells with receptors and give long-lasting coordinated responses (e.g. growth); chemical signalling is universal, even in bacteria. Arguments against: neural signalling is much faster and more precisely targeted; many responses need both, e.g. adrenaline release by nerves. Supported judgement: Each is effective for different purposes: chemical signals for widespread, sustained responses and nerves for rapid, precise ones. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: "Neonicotinoid pesticides should be banned to protect pollinators." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Precautionary restrictions such as the EU ban are justified, but alternatives and other causes of pollinator decline must also be addressed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they bind irreversibly to insect acetylcholine receptors and sublethal doses impair bee navigation; they persist in soil and water and affect non-target insects. Arguments against: they reduce crop losses and replacements may be more toxic or need spraying; evidence from field studies is mixed and other factors (Varroa, habitat loss) also harm bees. Supported judgement: Precautionary restrictions such as the EU ban are justified, but alternatives and other causes of pollinator decline must also be addressed.
